utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, if I could remind you of the affirmation that you made at the beginning of your evidence which still applies. Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just one problem from translator.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Is that all right? Your Honour, good afternoon. We reached a stage last night where we had been dealing with Rahovec and also with Lapusnik towards the end of July 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And you indicated that after the fall of Lapusnik large numbers of civilians fled the towns and the villages up into the mountains, and you yourself were warning them and helping them to do that. Now, I just want to deal with that episode, the episode of civilians in the mountains. Approximately how many thousand civilians ended up in the gorges and the mountains after the fall of Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we talk about the fall of the Lapusnik gorge, you have to bear in mind that it led also to Malisheve falling, too; they are connected. Around the mountains of Berisa at that time, there were about 50.000 people sheltered there, but the number kept increasing. In January to April 1999, that gorge, or those mountains, had about 85.000 inhabitants. The figures are, however, not official, but as the observers themselves noted and villagers who tried to keep numbers, they say that at the end there were about 85.000 civilians there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, in what way did you yourself assist these civilians in the gorges and in the mountains?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This event is linked to what I said yesterday. Seeing what was happening, I had started to organise in a way assistance from earlier on. I had started to collect foodstuff to keep them in time of danger, and what we had in a way foreseen came true. People left; they fled their homes without taking anything with them. They had --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: He wants me to repeat that they had fled their homes without taking anything with them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in order for them to escape Serbian shelling -- and we had to provide also for food for them, and we started to find places for them to take shelter, because on both sides of the Berisa Mountains there are numerous valleys where people could take refuge to escape shelling by the Serbian forces. And in these valleys and gorges, we started to set up some tents to distribute foodstuffs, food supplies, to the people. It is important to point out that we began to deploy soldiers at all these gorges and valleys in order for them to protect the population, in case the Serbian infantry attempted to penetrate the valleys and gorges because they couldn't do that by means of vehicles. But if they sent infantry troops, then we had to deploy our own soldiers to protect the population. These were more or less the ways we used to try and help and protect the population, and we continued to do that until the end of the war. Because of the stress, the concerns we had, because of the daily shelling, Your Honours, we started to feel under great pressure. You might imagine what life we could leave under these circumstances. In September I took the initiative to open a school for the kids who were there. There were kids starting from the age of 5, 6, 7, and 8, and they were under stress, they were afraid. And I wanted to give hope no the children and to their parents, and to divert their attention from the difficult life they were living in. So we talked with some teachers who happened to be there with their own families, and we took the initiative of opening up an improvised school for children to learn something there. And in those tents which various humanitarian organisations had provided to us, we started to, as I said, open up some school centres, if you like. You might imagine what kind of teaching that was, but it was an attempt on our part to try to divert the attention from daily stress and problems. One of those schools was visited by international reporters and journalists who filmed it and they made it public all over the world. We set up a kind of market-place of supplies for the population, so that those who were unable to have food supplies but had the money, they could buy some food provisions in this market because there were some people who managed to bring in food from various surrounding towns to supply this market-place. In this way people not only could buy food provisions but could try to forget deprivations and the difficulties they were faced with, not for a month or two, but for many months, even though the number of the population changed; sometimes it was greater, sometimes it was smaller. At a point in time, we had 15.000 then 30, 40.000 then the number reached 80.000 or 85.000. So in that small market-place people could buy food provisions, who could afford to do that. Those who couldn't, we started to supply them with those food reserves that I told you I had started to collect from earlier on. I wanted to tell you, Your Honours, there were 16 soldiers, 16 soldiers who were killed while attempting to go in -- back into the village and take from those villages some food supplies, some medicaments, clothes, and other necessary goods that they could find there. We tried to organise these operations at night. So 16 soldiers from my own unit got killed after September -- from September to May only while trying to get food supplies. Just to give you an example, it was by the -- at the end of August when the head of a family, who was acting as a leader of a neighbourhood, he had left his home, and those few food provisions he got with him, he had spent in the course of the last weeks, and now his children had nothing to live by. They started to cry, they wanted food, they wanted something to eat. And so that man was very desperate. This man is a businessman who before the war had a very huge capital, and even during the war he sold gas, construction materials, and food supplies. But at the time of the war, after the entry of the Serbian troops, he left everything behind and had just fled with his family. He came to me, we met by accident, and he asked me for help. Then I went to two soldiers of mine, talked with them, there was a small makeshift bakery, and I asked one of them, Do we have anymore flour? He said, Yes, we have flour to prepare to bake 20 loaves of bread. But these men that came to me, he was responsible for 200 people of his neighbourhood, and so we tried to supply all of them. We went to get corn somewhere else. We ground the corn and use some old mills which were out of use until then, and then they started to grind the corn and use for the civilian population. These were some of the things that we tried to do, to cope with the situation. This went on. Sometimes the situation got more tense, sometimes more -- less so. There were periods when humanitarian organisations helped us, but there also periods when we were left on our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I just want to take one more dimension of the assistance that you were rendering, and that is you have mentioned in passing the provision of medicaments. Were there medical centres set up alongside schools?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I couldn't call them medical centres, but there were -- they were improvised, makeshift, centres. In the tents there were some doctors who could provide medical service to the children and the population. There were thousands of children there. These doctors were general practitioners. One of them was a surgeon, and that surgeon performed surgery in the open, in the absence of the basic materials, supplies. We lacked all sorts of medicaments. After the Serb offensive, it was impossible to get medicaments from the cities, as we did before the Serbs had gotten control of these towns. The doctor -- and we have film of this. The doctor had to give some serums to the injured, and he to put that serum -- to hang it from an oak tree. There was a surgeon, as I said, there were some nurses, men and women who happened to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Do you just -- a matter of detail. Do you remember the names of any of the doctors?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. When we were there Agim Hazrolli often came to help. I'm talking the period after August, in September, October. Then there was Fadil Beka, but they moved to various places because they were wanted elsewhere. But permanently there was a paediatrician. His name was Besim Zogaj and another one Fitim Selimi in September, who came to Klecka from other part there. There was another doctor called Jakup, who was a dentist, I think, but he offered his services to the population. There were some seven, eight nurses. I remember one by the name of Drita who was there all the time, and she was from that village. And there was some other nurses whose names I can't recall at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I want to -- you have been describing the civilian population over the August, September, October period right the way through to the end of the war. I want to turn now to deal with your military activities in this same period. But first this question: By the end of July, what weaponry did you have available to you personally to use? Do you remember now? Can you specify what you had?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I had an automatic rifle, a Kalashnikov.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And what about the unit that you were attached to in Klecka up until the fall of Lapusnik and Malisheve?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My unit had a weapon, each of -- a personal weapon. We had a mortar, 150 millimetre. In July we received another mortar, 250 millimetre, I think it was the 10th or 12th of July, and we received it from Albania with a load of shipment -- with a shipment of arms. We had normally, hand-grenade, munitions. In July I think we also had some mines which Serbian troops had planted along the border, and the soldiers pulled them out and brought to us but we didn't know how to use them. Some might have a mortar, a machine-gun, and a sniper at this time in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, we know in August, passing on to this period you have been dealing with, the 121 Brigade as an area was established. Is there a date in your memory for the beginning of this move to establish a brigade, 121 Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was on the 6th of August, 1998, when Rexhep Selimi and Byslym Zyropi came to Klecke to see how things were after the offensive, which was still going on in various areas. They came with a concrete proposal, something which was approved by the General Staff, that is to form -- to start the forming of brigades in these area. The establishment of the Pastrik zone was rather delayed as a result of the offensive. So at this meeting there were some commanders of other units like Isak, Ismet, and Idriz, the commander of another unit whose last name I can't recall at this moment. He's from Obrinje and Krekov village. There was someone called Faik, a commander of another unit. And then there was Luan and another commander from Blace. So there were -- present at this meeting were commanders of various units. Byslym and Rexhep stayed that night in Klecke. They came, as I said, with a concrete proposal to form a brigade of all these units, and that brigade would have the name of Brigade 121, as a General Staff had decided. This brigade would be formed of all of the units located on both sides of the Berisa Mountains, meaning the units from Terpeze up to Guzace [phoen] or Blace. And on the other hand, the units that were situated from Lapusnik to Carraleve. Because by the time the Serbian forces had occupied all of other territories, with the exception of the valley where we were located. So the inhabitants had taken to the mountains of Klecka and Berisa after having abandoned their homes. So in the light of the reality and the situation on the ground, they said that we have to change the borders of the areas, the zones. So this region should have a unified unit in order for to us protect the Berisa Mountains and to prevent the Serbian troops from penetrating. So for that purpose, it was necessary to have a unified command as a logical development that might ensure us the necessary strength to protect the said territory. On the proposal of Rexhep and Byslym, I was appointed commander of Brigade 121. This decision was approved by all of the commanders of the units present there, and from this moment we started work to set up the structure of Brigade 121 with the borders that I mentioned yesterday. And from this moment on, parts of the territory that used to belong to Drenice Operational Zone now were part of Pastrik Operational Zone, which now had broader borders up to -- if you want me, I might describe it, up to Magure, because the territory covered by that brigade goes -- extends to that area. This brigade is formed as a result of three operational zones. Forming this brigade, including all these units, this brigade is part of Pastrik Operational Zone, and the later now becomes bigger and the borders are changed. It took some territory that used to belong to Drenice and Nerodime, and another part that was supposed to be part of Pastrik zone. This was for the first time a delineation of the borders and the establishment of a unified military unit, and for the first time I was the first commander of that brigade comprising all that territory that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, the proposal was the 6th of August. Can you give the Tribunal some idea how long it took to implement the proposal and make it an effective brigade area?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We encountered constant problems. We took immediate measures to set up the structure. First I started with the structure of the command, which was a normal development. On the next day, after consulting the commanders of the units, I proposed to the General Staff in consultation with Rexhep and Byslym that I have Kumanova, Ismet Jashari as well as my deputies, and Isak Musliu as the other, as assistant commander; and this is how we started our organisation. But our organisation was interrupted after 20 days as -- because of the other offensive mounted by the Serbian forces which came from the other part of the Berisa Mountains, from Duhle to Luzhnice. And on the 24th and 25th of August, the Serbian forces managed to penetrate into Klecke, something that interrupted our activity to expand and consolidate the Brigade 121. After Klecke fell on 25th of August, we were left with a very narrow space, area. I was 700 metres away at the time from the Serb forces where they were deployed and we didn't know where to stay. For two, three weeks we stayed -- slept out in the open. That was a powerful blow given to us. On the 24th, 25th of August, Kumanova was killed together with some other soldiers. There again some confusion was created. We were, as I said, in the process of consolidation and formation, so being under constant attacks we were unable to continue our efforts in this regard. After the penetration of the Serbian forces in Klecka on the 25th of August, people started to spread out. Some started to hide the weapons and to withdraw from that place, and there was a propaganda campaign saying that the KLA has withdrawn and so on. There were some soldiers, 12, actually, around me, and those 12 soldiers, one of them actually invited me to leave that place and to go on -- to another part of Drenica which were -- where the situation was calmer. He wanted me to be -- to stay there until the attack was over. I refused to leave the place, that place, telling him that I might leave that place only if I died. I couldn't do that because there were thousands of civilians there. I couldn't leave, myself, and abandon the population at the mercy of the Serbian forces. Among those civilians, Your Honours, was also my family. I could have withdrawn my family earlier from that area and from the war, but I never did that, because I consider it an amoral act to take care only of my family and leave the other citizens in the lurch. So during all that time, my family was among the surrounded civilian population, and together with those 12 soldiers, we started our work to re-establish Brigade 121. We wanted to show with our presence that we were there, that we were still existent. Some people said that I had left to Canada because they hadn't seen me for two or three days. It was a terrible propaganda we were subjected to. People were starting to panic, but we started our efforts to reorganise ourselves, and the bulk of the soldiers were waiting, what would happen. They had gone to their families to protect their families, but when they saw that I was there, when they saw that -- what I was about to do, when I told them that we had to reorganise ourselves again, as we did after the fall of Lapusnik gorge, they expressed their readiness to help and we started work to re-establish the brigade. This work continued up to the end of the war, because it was an ongoing process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Is it possible for you to indicate when you think the brigade was functioning satisfactorily? Is there a point in this period where when you could say it had been re-established and was functioning?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, yes; a satisfactory function, no. But according to the standards at that time, such a function was achieved after the signing of the Milosevic-Holbrook agreement. Because at that time this agreement created some space for us. Serbian forces withdrew from some points they had under their control until that time, for example, from Klecka, because as of 25th of August Serb forces were stationed in Klecka until the Milosevic-Holbrook agreement. When the Serb forces withdrew from this position with the signing of the agreement, our situation consolidated. And as of November, I can say that the brigade functioned satisfactorily and functioned well in that part, that is to say, in the Pastrik Operational Zone. Because the blows we had suffered in August, we overcame these blows, and it was easier now -- for us now to be organised, unlike some other units when they had to be organised from scratch. This is did not happen with us. I didn't have at any time problems with soldiers to organise them; I always had problems with the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: We know that in November you were appointed to the General Staff, and the question is: To what extent did you continue with your involvement with Brigade 121 after that appointment?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, the developments in August had created an emotional link between us. We didn't abandon each other. We stood by each other. We had protected the civilian population, and this was the outcome of a joint effort and we were proud of it. And this connection continued. The appointment from General Staff -- or better to say I was informed about this on the 28th of November, on the day of the flag, on a manifestation that I had organised in Klecka with the soldiers from my brigade. And in the first days of December, I participated for the first time in the meetings of the General Staff as a member of the General Staff. However, my activities and my connections with the Brigade 121 continued even after my appointment. Although another person was appointed to replace me, I always had connections with the brigade. At any time when there were fightings, I communicated with the brigade or I participated together with the soldiers in those fightings, and this continued until I left for Albania. I could never separate from my brigade. I knew the soldiers of my brigade. Although as of November I was a member of the General Staff, soldiers from 121 Brigade considered me their commander until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to turn in a moment to events towards the end of the war after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if this might therefore be an appropriate moment to show the short film of the places he has been talking about. We've made arrangement so that it can be operated from this side. The suggestion is since Mr. Limaj knows the places in the film -- I make it clear, it was not filmed by him, obviously. It has been filmed very recently. So obviously there may have been some changes, but it's just to give an idea of the layout of the landscape and the places. There are at various moments written onto the screen in Albanian headings in the hope of indicating the area to be covered in that section of film. Could I also say to Mr. Limaj if he could add a commentary -- a slow commentary - it's going to be difficult to keep up otherwise - as to the places that we're dealing with, particularly if it's not entirely clear. If you need it stopped -- may I just check who's going to be stopping it so we know who to indicate -- oh right. We have control at this side, we hope. So if you need to stop it, can you do so. So may I ask for the film to start running now. Yes -- sorry. I think it may be -- yes, the computer monitor, yes, should be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours , the interpreters kindly ask you whether we are supposed to interpret anything during this film?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: The answer is: Yes, please. It will just be what is said by Mr. Limaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you would interpret what is said by Mr. Limaj, please. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I just have a point of inquiry. Maybe it's being addressed at the moment, looking at the screen. I'm wondering if there is any way to put a counter on -- make it visible, otherwise the comments are not going -- there's going to be a very poor record about what he is talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yeah, I think there is a monitor at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there no way of coordinating, though commentary with the monitor, Mr. Mansfield? Unless somebody calls at significant intervals the number being displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think -- yes, that's, Your Honour, if I may say so, a perfectly acceptable suggestion. And perhaps if my junior were to call out the monitor number at the stage of the particular commentary because we have it on a smaller screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, here is the Komorane crossroads on which Serbian forces were constantly positions, and from Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this place the attacks were launched. This place was a checkpoint where the forces themselves were positioned in the vicinity, and they came often to this location. On the upper part, there is a part of Lapusnik visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that's at 25 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If possible, if you can rewind it, yes, here. If you can stop it here, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 54 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these are the mountains that we refer to as Berisa Mountains seen from the part of Drenoc municipality. The range of mountains start from Carraleve. They are interrupted by the main road to Lapusnik, but they continue, the range continues to Drenica. If you see the peak here, this hill, this is the location where the Serb forces were positioned after the fall of Lapusnik gorge. The Serbs were positioned here, and they withdrew from this position after the Milosevic-Holbrook agreement was signed, which was, if I'm not mistaken, around the 15th of October. And the Serbs, from this position, and downhill had their checkpoints, and from these positions they were guarding the main road. On the 9th of May, they realised that the only way they could protect the main road was for them to go higher up on the hill so that they could control the main road better. Because on the 9th of May, we descended from this place, from this rock, when we attacked them. And therefore they assumed this -- they took up this position, a strategic one, in order to protect and have under control their -- the main road.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This here is called Quka e Komoranit. It's a location where the Yugoslav army, not only during the events in 1998 but throughout the time, used it as a military base, training base, during spring. In the period in question, they were positioned on this location. This is, as the crow flies, about 500 -- 3 to 4 kilometres from Lapusnik gorge and from the mountains that we saw earlier. This is a hill and a strategic place which -- from where you can see clearly all of the villages in the valleys around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's 4 -- at 1 minute and 4 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a view from Quka e Komoranit where the Yugoslav army was positioned. As you can see, this is Lapusnik as a village. That is a focus, the zoom of the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: At 1 minute and 18 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a broader view, also focussed on Lapusnik, but on the left-hand side, which cannot be seen here, there are situated the villages of Kizhareke, Sedlare, and Kroimire. On the right side, you can see Lapusnik village entirely, and you can see that it's quite a big village and has a broad area around it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, Your Honours, earlier, the Serbian police and military forces were positioned at Quka e Komoranit and this is the area that they shelled during the offensives, especially on the 24th and 25th of July. From this position, they applied the -- their artillery against the Lapusnik, not only the village but against the entire region.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you can see -- a hill on the left side. You can see that the terrain is bare. There are no trees at all, and it continues in this manner up to the zone which was entirely under Serb attack. And from the rock and to different points as of 25th of August, Serbian forces set up their positions and checkpoints up to the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: At 2 minutes and 44 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you could pause it here. From this position, you can clearly see the peak that I explained earlier, where the Serb positions were, and you can see that some houses, and you can see the village of Kizhareke, Nekovce, and Shale. These were the locations that were attacked by the Serb forces, infantry, and tanks, and the civilian population from these villages then withdrew up to the mountains because they didn't have -- where to go from this part here, because then they would be directly a target of Serbian forces, but they withdraw in the direction of the mountains in the nearest gorges as in the gorge of Divjak and Klecke. The villagers knew these gorges because they had always lived in their vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 3 minutes and 22 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, here you can see the bare terrain from the peak, from the strategic point going down. I forget to mention it earlier. This is the so-called Guri i Gradines that we have so often heard about during this trial. So this is the bare part of the mountain. The other part was -- is what we call Lluga. It's not actually a forest; it's a thorny place, place with thorns, a territory with shrubs. And later on the Serbs took control of all this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 3 minutes and 43 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are the surrounding villages, Kishna Reka, Nekovce, and other villages that I mentioned. Maybe it's not necessary to pause it here. From this angle, you cannot see the village ever Klecke. You can see the villages on the foot of the mountains which were Nekovce, Shale, Bajice, up to Pjetershtice village and Carraleve. At that time, all these villages were included in the fightings and attacked by the Serb forces. They -- the Serb forces were moving towards these villages, and the entire population from these villages then took to the mountains after the offensive.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the geographical area comprising of some 15 kilometres, if I'm not wrong, maybe even more, it shows the surrounding the ridges, the range of mountains, and the valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: At 4 minutes and 13 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Goles, in the upper part. The antenna that you can see known as the strongest base of Yugoslavia after the 1990s. This was a position where the Serbian army always used. This area was prohibited for civilians; civilians could not go to that area. The army had this base as of 1990s, and it was the strongest base. The entire territory of the villages that you saw previously could be seen from this area, and from this area we were constantly shelled in the direction of Klecka with rocket launchers. This was one of the first targets of NATO after the bombing campaign started because it was a very powerful military base.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 4 minutes and 43 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are the last Serbian positions at Komorane before reaching Lapusnik village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From another angle, again the last positions of the Serbs. Your Honours, here there is a stream, a small stream, that divided the Serbian positions before they entered Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Previously you could clearly see the peak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is part of one of the neighbourhoods of Lapusnik village. This area then continues in the direction of Guri i Gradines, the rock.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Guri i Gradines where the Serb forces were positioned, and from this point we walked down when we attacked the Serb forces. So after the 26th of July, in order to have control over the main road, the Serb forces positioned themselves on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: At 6 minutes and 42 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I'm not mistaken, from the KLA positions on Lapusnik gorge, this is a view from there. This is the main road into the direction of Peja, going to the direction of Peja, and you can see the houses of Lapusnik village as scattered in different neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 7 minutes and 11 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the guri in Lapusnik. If you recall from yesterday, I said that the Serbian troops had taken a strategic position here. It was precisely here in this place, it's a stone, guri, in Albanian, like the Guri i Gradines. From that high position we had seen the Serbs, and we went down to this place to attack the Serbian forces. From here, you could have a very good view of the main road, and the entire area where the KLA units were being attacked. So from Gradines we attacked this place on the first day we attacked the Serbs on the 9th of May. So the Serbs knew that in order to protect the main road, they had to be deployed up there in order to feel secure here at Lapusnik Guri, or rock.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I'm not mistaken, I see these two signs, Guri i Gradines and Guri Lapusnik. There are some houses here, and this is the place that I mentioned yesterday of the house that I visit, Qerkini's house that I visited. It must be somewhere in this area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are the houses. If we could rewind it a little bit. This part of the houses on the left, you could have a better view of them here. Could you please continue, play it on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the place. When I told you yesterday that I visited a kitchen in the house, this is near -- in the vicinity of this rock, this guri, the place we ate lunch, that improvised kitchen, the place where we stayed in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From here, Your Honours, from the other place you could have a very small view, whereas from here it's a hill, a very steep hill. From this part, I think this is where the last neighbourhood of Lapusnik is situated, bordering the mountains, Berisa Mountains. You have to climb, it's a very steep terrain. It's a small rise because during the Serb regime they destroyed all the mountains, the hills, they divested them of any green -- of any vegetation. They sold the timber, and as you see the place is very bare, because prior to the 1990s it was very dense with foliage and forest. But after the 1990s, as you see, it became bare. The timber was exported and -- or sold to the local inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no need for me to make a comment; it's part of Lapusnik seen from the Berisa Mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 8 minutes and 49 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is the view you can have of this place from the Gradines rock, or guri, you -- from here you can have -- from the Guri i Gradines you can have a view of the Prishtine-Peja highway -- road. This is the place from where we attacked the Serbian forces. It's a rather broader view of Lapusnik village up to the hill that borders it. The road divides, if I could say, the mountain range. You can see not only the Lapusnik village, but all the surrounding villages from here. You could see the valley in the other part of Drenice. You could see that part with shrubs. You can have an idea of the height of the mountains and the bare terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 9 minutes and 8 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the Gradines rock, you can have a view of the villages in the direction of Quka e Komorane from another angle, as you can see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this place, in this very place, after the 26th of July the Serbs were deployed here. And from here, they could control the entire Lapusnik and the -- and the surrounding areas and the valley as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see here. This is the view you have, Your Honours, of the Gradines rock and the direction of Berisa and Klecke. You cannot see the Berisa village here, let alone Klecke which is in the hinterland. But from here the Serbs could control the entire ground -- area. We could not -- we had to remove the civilian population in the direction of the villages in the valleys of Kishna Reka and Nekovce, because all this area was fired -- was under constant fire by the Serb troops. From here, to where we were, there was a -- like a buffer zone. We couldn't move there because we were under the attack of the Serb forces. From here they had complete control of the area, the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 10 minutes and 54 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the direction from Gradines rock to Klecke, Guri.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It takes about two hours from here to go there if you take the direction directly -- I mean, as the crow flies it might take five hours, but if you take other paths, shorter ones, it can take you two hours to reach there. Of course I'm talking if you walk on foot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the Gradines rock, you can see Komorane crossroads. It's not clear to me either, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not clear from position we are looking at it. It may be after a while I can make it out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the Gradines rock, you can see Gllogovc town. There is a ferrous nickel plant in Gllogovc where the Serbian forces were deployed. There was rumours it was a form of concentration camp, but this is where the Serbs were deployed, Drenoc of Gllogovc town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 12 minutes and 5 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the main road, direction of Peja and Prishtine from Komorane.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we come from Drenoc, you come to Komorane; on the left you can go to Pristina, on the right to Peja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 13 minutes and 12 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe it's written here, I don't know. This is the -- Orlate crossroads or Kryqi. Your Honours, from Lapusnik the road to Orlate, as you can see on this signboard, this is the turn to Malisheve. There was a military unit stationed here; it patrolled -- usually patrolled the road after the Lapusnik gorge fell. And this village, Orlate, as you can see, it was part of the Drenica Operational Zone. I believe we can see it better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 13 minutes and 23 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you can rewind it just for a second, please. No, no. Fast-forward it a little bit. A little bit more, yes it's okay here. You can pause here. Your Honours, this is the asphalt road that takes from Orlate to Malisheve, and this is the road that enters in the direction of Terpeze, Novoselle, Klecke. Yesterday I told you that we went from Terpeze, when I went to Malisheve. So the population coming from Malisheve, they entered this area through Terpeze to get to the mountains. So myself and others, whenever we travelled from Klecka, we used this road, went to Orlate. And from Orlate, using the asphalt road, we continued to Lapusnik, because this was in the inner part of the territory and there was no risk from the Serbian forces. So at all times by vehicles when we travelled by vehicles, our movement from Klecka to Lapusnik was via this road. After the fall of the Lapusnik gorge, as I said yesterday, some of the commanders, amongst them myself, we gathered in order to set up some positions, military positions, in order to be able to resist and to prevent the Serbs from penetrating the villages, to abandon the main road and enter the villages, because a large number of people were stationed there; and on the other side, if the Serbs enters Terpeze that would block us fully. If you can see this place here, on the left side, from the 27th and 28th of August, in this house, in this location, and up to the end of the war, the Serb positions -- the Serb police, correction, was positioned in this house. So from the 27th of July, the Serb forces were constantly here. Now we have a view from the other side of the Berisa Mountains. In addition, this place is called Smonice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 13 minutes and 36 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The road that shows Klecka direction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what we previously saw was the village of Terpeze as seen immediately from the road.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, this is the village of Terpeze. You can see the gorges here. From these parts, the civilian population enters the inner part of the village and then disperses in the gorges. So the journey was to go directly to Novoselle and then to penetrate via the villages of Lladrovc and the surrounding villages. This road continues to Klecka, from Terpeze village to Klecka. And it's here where we build up this defence line in order to defend the population. And we had second positions, if -- in case we withdrew from these positions, to continue the resistance from the second positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 14 minutes and 5 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can pause here. This is my base, Your Honours. Now we are in Klecke. This is a house where I stayed, and from this house Jakup Krasniqi gave the statement. The window looking at us, that is the window from where the spokesperson gave his statement. This is a house of my nephews, and I stayed in this house during the entire time up until December. Here I would like to separate the period from the 25th of August, when the positions were taken by the Serb forces, which lasted until the signing of the Holbrook-Milosevic agreement. But for this period, I -- up to December, I stayed in this house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 14 minutes and 22 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a bakery. I would like to use opportunity -- correction, this is a place that was used by my nephews for limestone, burning of limestone. For some time, this was the only way for someone to provide for their families. So the only way was to sell limestone, especially, in the 1980s and 1990s. And every family had their limestone oven. That's why I wanted this picture to be in the film so that I can explain this to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 14 minutes and 29 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are the houses near my base. As I mentioned yesterday, we had enough space where soldiers could stay. And as for the allegations that some corpses were burned in Klecke, I asked the General Staff to conduct an investigation about this and to refer the cause to The Hague investigators or to bring an independent commission to verify the truth. The General Staff at that time asked for such a thing, but the Serbs caused some problems. I think that a Finnish team arrived, but I don't know what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 14.37. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This wall continues downwards - you don't have to pause - this is the compound that belongs to my nephews, Your Honours. This is the yard, their yard. You can continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this entire area with this wall belongs to my nephews. Everything that is inside the walls belongs to these young men, and that's why I was permitted to stay here with my people. This is Klecke, as I described it earlier. The houses are scattered, and from here you can also see the village of Divjak. You can see some houses of Divjak and some of Klecke. Klecka has no more houses than these than you can see on the picture. As I said yesterday, Klecka identifies with my nephews, because most of it is inhabited but my nephews.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time. It might be convenient to break at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mansfield. We will resume at five minutes past 4.00

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, if we could continue, there's a little more film to see. And the same procedure as before, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Recommencing at 14 minutes and 53 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you can see a gorge on the right-hand side of this house. This is one of the gorges where the civilian population was sheltering after August and later on, even before August, after the gorge was penetrated. After August, except for this position, the Serb forces were also positioned in the entire area; they established their own points. And we did not have any possibility to take our positions. We had to penetrate inside the gorges and create there our positions and defend the population. These houses in these villages were under Serb control for two months. The villages in the direction of Novoselle and Divjak village on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 14 minutes and 56 seconds

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see here Goleshi; it's higher than Klecka. From here, I said it earlier that the Serbian forces shelled here -- from here uninterruptedly on this village, on this part. Sometime around the 20th or the 22nd, but especially after the 25th of July, this was shelled from Goleshi, because Goleshi it's much higher than Klecka and this area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 15 minutes and 15 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This road leads to the villages of Javora and Luznica. Javora and Luznica are villages in the municipality of Suhareke. This is the boundary between the municipalities. This is the Lipjan municipality. Klecka for some time was part of the Lipjan municipality and then became part of the Malisheve municipality. They decided themselves to become part of the Malisheve municipality, the villagers, I mean. While Javora in this direction and Luznica remained in the Suhareke municipality. So here is the boundary between Lipjan, Suhareke, Malisheve, and Drenoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 15 minutes and 24 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the houses you can see here are houses of my relatives, of my nephews.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a stable. My nephews had at the time this stable. They at the time had around 500 sheep, they also had cows, and this is the stable. I think that now it has the same function, but it serves as a cowshed more because they don't have sheep anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 15 minutes and 47 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the entrance, the entrance of my base where I stayed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the yard which goes downhill.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 16 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you could stop it here. Honoured Judges, if you could see here, this is a new house, it has been built recently, while the houses below that house they were built before the war. As I said, we decided to base ourselves in Klecka because it was a safe place for us, and the situation was such that we could stay there without being detected by others. So this is how far our families' houses were from the place where I stayed. Because these people had workers working for them. Somebody worked as a shepherd who cared for the sheep, others worked as farmers, so it was practical for us to have our nephews pick up the food for us. And because they had workers there, nobody would ask questions why they needed the food. So it was not extraordinary for them to move from -- to move up and down and go and find food and nobody would ask questions. That's why I want to give just one example. On the 9th of May, when we came out publicly and we were known as members of the KLA the villagers saw us, the villagers of Klecka, one of my relative, of my nephew's relatives in Klecka, his house is here in this group of houses, because these people that lived here they are close relatives. So one of them told us -- he said that, I have been to Drenica for a week and slept there in Drenica, only to see a member of the KLA, and I did not know that you were here in my village. You have been here very close to us and I didn't know it. So this shows that the degree of secrecy and how we went about undetected. Even the houses that you can see here, one of the houses, a white, one here on the front -- on the forefront, and two others below that, these are houses of my relatives, of my nephews - even this on the right side - while two or three other houses belonged to their relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 16 minutes and 7 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is the gorge. This is the gorge where the civilians stayed. If you could -- can see the houses below, this is the village of Shale, or Sedlare, but it's far away from here. And the civilian population from these villages, they entered this gorge, and we set up a defensive circle from Shale to Klecka, each when Klecka was occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 16 minutes and 13 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You can see here the distance. This is the gorge, the valley, from the distance. It is difficult to see from this distance, but maybe the cameraman could not approach it anymore. This gorge belongs to the Sedlare village, or Shale village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go on. These are houses of the Klecka village. These are dispersed houses but they are the same ones that we have seen before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can explain here, Honourable Judges. When I say "houses," I mean households because some of them are compounds. When I say a house, it means in fact a compound which is under one head of household. It belongs -- they belong to one person. Even the compound of my nephews included four or five houses, but these are houses that belong to one head of household.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 17 minutes and 12 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can go on because I don't have any comment about this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you can see the arrow that shows the direction from where you can see Lapusnik. Of course, Lapusnik cannot be seen from here, not even Novoselle or Shatiri [phoen] neither Berisa, because it's very far from here and the terrain is such that you cannot see it. But the direction is this: To go to Lapusnik and Novo Selo and Terpeze, if you go through the mountains, then you get to Novo Selo first and then Berisa. And of course I explained to you how we went to attack the main road, Peja-Pristina, but these were secondary roads, not main roads. These were roads that were paths that were used by the villagers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All these houses were burned down after the Serbian forces penetrated here. They were all burnt and destroyed. So they have been reconstructed or sometimes repaired if there were walls that remained after the war. Some of them were repaired by us, the soldiers, after November, when we entered Klecka after the Serbian forces left. For example, it was ourselves, the soldiers, that repaired the base where we stayed, the house where we stayed, after the Serbian forces left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 22 minutes and 43 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up to now we were looking at the Lipjan commune, the part that is in the direction of the Lipjan -- sorry, municipality. Now we see in the direction of Malisheve municipality. So in your focus here, you can see the villages of the Malisheve municipality, and the mountains there are mountains of the Suhareke municipality. So this is the other part of the Berisa Mountains or Klecka. This village on the far left - you can see the houses here - is the Belanica village. We might see it by -- closer earlier, but in this direction, if you go in this direction, you would be able to see my birth place, my village. While -- here at the foot of the mountain here, you cannot see it, but there is a village here which is the Senik village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 23 minutes and 3 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is the road, yes. There is one here, one road here, which is asphalted road. This road comes towards the direction of the village Senik. There are some other roads or paths but they are very difficult roads, dirt roads, used by the villagers when they went to gather firewood and so on. As I said, the deforestation started after 1990. And this plain or this meadow that you can see here, there are vineyards here; they were part of the socialist cooperatives in the past. And there was one enterprise here, a farming enterprise, and there were about 500 or 600 villagers who worked there. So all of it is a vineyard, the whole territory. But after 1990, the workers were fired and the vineyard was destroyed. So it was left there like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 23 minutes and 19 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now you can see clearly the Senik village, and the road leads to Banje, the village of Banje. Honourable Judges, in July, during the offensive, the Serbian forces came up to here, up to Senik village, and this plain you can see here was full of weaponry, Serbian weaponry. They came up to here, and the Senik village was under their control. They practically surrounded the whole mountain here, from both sides, from Malisheve and Lipjan. You can see here my neighbourhood as well; it's the first neighbourhood on the right. It's a little darker and some houses can be seen of my neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 23 minutes and 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is a close-up. If you can see, there's a big building here, which is the school. I completed my primary education here, and this is part of the village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see here most of the villages of the Malisheve municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I'm not mistaken, this is Malisheve, as far as I can see -- no, it isn't, because there is a mosque here. It must be Belanica, because Malisheve does not have a mosque.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the Lladrovc village. The Serbian forces were here as well, and the whole civilian population from here, from these villages, went to the Klecka mountains for shelter. So villagers from Malisheve municipality, my village, they went towards the mountains of Klecka in the gorges, and they had the same defence system that we had on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 24 minutes and 5 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the Senik village I mentioned earlier. The Serbian forces came here to Klecka. The civilian population left, and the Serbian forces shelled with a tanks -- with their tanks this village in order for their infantry to be able to enter the village. They killed a whole family here, a family of 11 members, a woman and a little child, so it was because of Serbian shelling 11 civilians were killed immediately. This was the largest loss we had in civilians, the largest number of casualties. There were also other people killed. We also had wounded people but not to that degree. And this is the mill, if you can see here. It's in the middle of the village, the tall building. And we went -- this is the place I told you we went to get flour for the civilian population. From -- we went from the mountains to this mill to get supplies. After we got all the flour then we had -- there was some grain sacks there that we took as well. But this happened later, not in August, neither in September, maybe April -- or March or April 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 24 minutes and 25 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here is a view in the direction of Shtime or Carraleve and Kroimire. Behind the mountains, the mountains in the far end, if you get on top of those, you can see Kroimire and other villages, Carraleve and then Shtime, so they are behind those mountains. While on this side you will find the villages of Duge, Karaqice. I'm not sure where they belonged to the Shtime or Lipjan community -- sorry, municipality, but I think they belonged to the Lipjan municipality. I'm not a hundred per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 24 minutes and 31 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the Lladrovc gorge. As you can see, the population, the civilian population came into this gorge for shelter. There are seven or eight gorges in this area where the population -- civilian population was sheltered. If can you see here in the far left, you can see Malisheve. Now you can see Malisheve.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 24 minutes and 40 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you could stop here. Honourable Judges, this is the martyrs' cemetery, soldiers that have laid down their lives, soldiers of the 121 Brigade. These were soldiers that belonged to various units before, but then those units became part of the 121 Brigade. And they were considered martyrs of this brigade although they might have been killed before the brigade was formed. So here, there are around 70 martyrs that have been buried, people who were killed during the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 25 minutes and 8 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the road from the village Novoselle or Shatiri. From here you can see Klecka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's from this memorial complex that you can see where Klecka and where my base was, because the complex is between the Klecka village and Shatiri or Novo Selo village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the same view. This shows the terrain, the places where we sheltered the population. From here, in 28 minutes or half an hour you can get to my village, of course by car.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 25 minutes and 55 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is Novoselle or Shatiri you can see here the houses that are dispersed all over the terrain. I don't know how many houses or households it has.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 26 minutes and 16 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A little further. Your Honours, you can see here the entrance to Rahovec. If you can see this ridge here, the soldiers were here, the soldiers that got into Rahovec and the units. And if you could go further with the images. This is the road that comes from Malisheve to Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 26 minutes and 53 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you could stop here, please. This is the road that I mentioned yesterday, the road that leads downtown -- to downtown Rahovec and the other one that leads outside town. The other one is the ring road; it goes by Rahovec and then you can go to Prizren. So when I mentioned yesterday that I went to Rahovec, I meant this ring road that goes by Rahovec but not -- does not go into the centre of Rahovec. The house on the left here, three-storeyed house. This is the house where I met those soldiers with whom I spoke about what was going on. And the next day, when I met Agim Qelaj and same the Zyropi -- and maybe I'm wrong about the name, but it was also Musa and Rexhep. It was here that I met them. And Agim improvised here some kind of headquarters for those two days because the General Staff had appointed him a commander for this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 27 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is the road that goes by the town, it does not go into the centre, and this is where I travelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 27 minutes and 11 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can go on with the images.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's okay here. When I said yesterday, Your Honours, that we went towards the road in order not to leave the -- not to let the Serbian forces enter Rahovec. So this is a -- a small bridge and there's a stream down here, but it was difficult to build a defence line here to protect the civilians. So if we can see here on the computer, on your left, that's where we started to dig some trenches. And there's where I stayed with the 12 soldiers and some soldiers came later, some other soldiers came later. And that was the resistance line, as we called it. I stayed there until I got sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 28 minutes and 15 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is the ridge. I said there's a kind of a ridge where we stayed, but there were Serbian snipers here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 28 minutes and 25 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the crossroads. Maybe you should go further with the images a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 28 minutes and 33 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, here. This is the crossroads, Your Honours. On your left, the road leads to Rahovec; you can get into Rahovec. So on your right, that is the road that goes towards Malisheve. And that's the ring road that does not get in the -- does not go into the centre of Rahovec, and this is where I met those 12 soldiers. And I said that the Serbs shelled here. It was exactly where this yellow car is, where the Serbs shelled, and I was there with the 12 soldiers. And we left only a couple of minutes before the shells fell here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 28 minutes and 36 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is an illustration that shows the direction towards Pristina, the entrance to Rahovec. And the road that comes from Gjakova on the right side, and the other one goes towards Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 28.44. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can go on. This is the town of Rahovec. It's -- this image is taken from a hill. This is an old town, but it's a very dense town, as you can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 29 minutes and 58 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the town of Malisheve, Your Honours; it's a small town. It used to be a big village; it's now called a small town. When the Serbian forces penetrated here on the 25th of July, 25th to the 27th of July, during the summer offensive, this village or this small town was totally burned down, razed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: 30 minutes and 46 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's I think the end of the film because it's -- may I thank my co-counsel for his very adept control through the film.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Will you tender the -- I'm not sure what format you have it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: A DVD, yes. It is in fact -- I will get the number, if it can be exhibited now, or give it a number now anyway. The item we're up to DL9, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Defence Exhibit DL9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Limaj, I want to turn now in the final stages to some developments towards the end of the war and after the war, and I'll do them by topic heading. The first one is the Rambouillet talks and what happened after that. Do you remember when they were, just roughly?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it might be appropriate that I mention here after I became a member of the General Staff, I was appointed chief of military police. As for Rambouillet talks, in February 1999, after the massacre at Recak where the Serb forces killed more than 40 civilians, the international community took urgent steps in organising a peace conference for Kosova, and the KLA, its General Staff, engaged for this conference and decided to take part in it. The Albanian delegation consisted of the political staff of the KLA. At the time, I was a member of the General Staff. I was in Kosova. I made sure that we reached a peaceful agreement in Rambouillet. It is a public knowledge now, this fact, that talks in Rambouillet lasted for two weeks but they did not conclude with the signing of a peaceful agreement because there were members of the units who were net yet clear about the importance of that agreement. They were rather confused and unclear. Of course this was the doing of certain persons. Therefore, they demanded that the Kosova delegation return to Kosova to make clear to the people the importance of this agreement. Some of us who were members of the General Staff in Kosova tried to convince the people that the delegation in Rambouillet represents the KLA, has full authority, and that we should support its stance. The decision to take part in Rambouillet I think was most important. I think this is where I played a crucial role regarding the participation in such a peaceful conference, which after all was our goal, to come to the face when we could resolve once and for all the question of the status of Kosova. But as you know, the Serbs refused to accept the agreement of Rambouillet and after the delegation returned to Kosova and made further consultations. All the zone commanders agreed with this peaceful agreement and authorised our delegation to sign such an agreement. The Serbs did not sign it, and this led to the NATO air strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And following the conference, were you given a particular role and appointed as a particular minister?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kosova delegation, in its constant efforts to unify the Albanian political factors there, such efforts had been going on during all the wartime and it was also the insistence of the international community that the Albanians had a unified delegation in order to form a government with representatives from all the political forces. Apparently the Albanians in Rambouillet agreed to form a joint government with representatives of the KLA, LDK, the movement for democratic unity - I'm not sure about the name it was called at that time - and some independent interlocutors. So they had agreed to form a government. The chairman of the delegation in Rambouillet was Mr. Hashim Thaqi from the KLA. He was the one that chaired the delegation, the Albanian delegation, in the talks. So they agreed that the person who would form a joint Albanian government should be a KLA representative; in this case, it was the leader of the political leadership, Mr. Thaqi. And they had divided also the ministries, the Ministry of Defence, of order, and some other ministries that they had thought to give to the representatives of the KLA. And in this case, I was elected to be a deputy minister of defence of the provisional government it was called then. This occurred in April -- April, May, end of April, I think, beginning of May, if I'm not wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. I think just to make clear, we are now in 1999? That's right.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, always in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And if I may, just move forward. Were you also engaged in talks for the demilitarisation of the KLA clearly towards the end of the war itself?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the departure, the withdrawal, of the Serb forces and the Kumanova agreement, the entry of the NATO forces in Kosova, international representatives - in this case NATO representatives - and a KFOR commander for Kosova; as well as international diplomats; the former spokesperson of the state department, James Rubin, of the delegation; together with some NATO officers headed by Mr. Jackson, in order to demilitarise the KLA. They demanded that the KLA be demilitarised, hand over its -- surrender its weapons, and go home. In these talks, I was a direct participant together with the chairman of the government, Mr. Thaqi; the Chief of Staff of KLA, who at that time was Agim Qelaj; and for some time present were also some zone commanders. But then the talks were continued by us. And we came to the conclusion in a week to sign an agreement on the demilitarisation and transformation of the KLA, an agreement which we signed at the KFOR base. The NATO forces entered Kosova on the 12th, and we signed this agreement on the demilitarisation, transformation of the KLA on the 17th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And in relation to this exercise, were you, yourself, personally thanked by those who had participated for the contribution you had made to achieving this result?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in many instances -- I have people who have followed developments, various analysts, various international organisations have expressed their -- their pleasure at what was done at that time. Because it was obvious that the aim, the goal, of the KLA was to liberate the country. Now that the Serb forces had withdrawn, we were willing to return to normal life. I want to stress, however, that we didn't want to demilitarise the KLA immediately because we didn't know what to do with the forces, but to transform it gradually, to retain a force which would be looked upon by the citizen as a protection core. And this demand was going to be fulfilled after the demilitarisation process. So for the three-month period, from June to September, the demilitarisation of the units of the KLA would take place, then talks should be held on a possibly transformation of the KLA, and joint group of the joint staff of the KLA and NATO was formed to demilitarise the KLA over a three-month period. After three months this commission thought that the demilitarisation was successful and complete and then talks continued for some more time. We visited London, Brussels, Rome, Washington, to present our views why it was important for a -- a body represented by members of the KLA that would be considered as a protection force by the people in general. We managed to find the understanding of such international centres during our visits and thanks to the constructive work we had done in cooperation with the international community, we managed to transform the KLA, to form a protection corps in Kosova which would deal with the protection of people's interest in case of emergencies, in case of dangers. Serve as a protective measure in general. The mandate of this force is not very clear. It is meant to be a civilian emergency corps, but a force that will have a more well defined the mission at a future phase. So the fate of this organisation depends on the final definition of the Kosova status. We managed to sign such an agreement with General Clark and Jackson, but it was also endorsed by the international community, something that led to the creation of the Kosovo protection corps which for us was a major victory because we managed to retain a form of organisation, a military organisation, that would provide guarantees for the future. The agreement on demilitarisation foresees that part of the members of the KLA remain with the Kosovar protection corps. You can imagine, Your Honours, to form an army within a year, to fight and then within the same year to demilitarise it, to disband it, this is something that has never occurred in the history of mankind. For a body, for an organisation to be formed, to perform its function and then to demilitarise it, I think this is a concrete example to show that none of these people wanted to take arms because they wished to do so but just because they wanted to drive out the Milosevic violent regime. And after that, they had no reason to stick to their weapons. After that, all of them returned to their daily life. So as I said, we foresaw that some of the forces remain with the Kosovar protection corps, whereas the political wing of the KLA should form a political party to start the political activity in the conditions of Free Kosova. The political wing formed the political party which is called the Democratic Party of Kosovo started the establishment of its respective structures all over Kosovo to prepare it to take part in the election and to contribute the institutional building of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And it right to say that you participated in a number of elections that followed, both local and at national level?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was elected the secretary for public relations after the establishment of this party. I was the person who had authority to communicate with the public until election came. I participated in the first local election, democratic election held in 2000. I ran in the context of the Democratic Party for Pristina communal assembly. In 2001 I participated in the electoral campaign and ran as a deputy for the Kosova assembly in the context of the proportional list of the Democratic Party of Kosova. And in 2002, again I ran for Pristina communal assembly. So I participated directly in three elections held in Kosova until then, and I was elected as a member of the assembly, even though we wanted to win, but it was the vote of the citizens that decided. Then I was elected as department to the assembly of Kosova from where I came here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I want to at this stage, if I may, these are the final exhibits. If you'd just look at two exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there are translations of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Would you identify what they are and when you have we will ask that they be exhibited. They both concern elections. Copies have already been provided to everybody. There are two separate document there is. I have given you an original of one and a copy of the other one. One is your candidacy for the mayor of Pristina, and the other one is -- contains your photograph on it. It's a coloured brochure and you have it in your hand at the moment. And it has a number of exhortations within it and observations within it. Which is the first, in terms of time? There were three elections so which of the -- these documents relates to the first election?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This brochure, Your Honours, which has on the front page my picture, it's a kind of propaganda material, which gives some information about my person. It was prepared during the first local election of 2000 for the city of Pristina. This paper here, which is a kind of leaflet addressed to the citizens, we used to distribute it to every house, it dates 2002 to the local elections at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I wonder if in fact to save having a proliferation these two documents could become DL10. With translations. There are translations already provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence Exhibit for candidate profile of Fatmir Limaj for mayor of Pristina and translation will be given exhibit number DL10. And the next one which is the PDK leaflet of Fatmir Limaj and translation will be given exhibit number DL11.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you this question for a particular reason, which may be obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: During those years - that is, 1999, 2000, 2001, 2002 - did you appear on many occasions Kosovo national television in relation to your position politically?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: During 1998, 1999, I had appeared on television. As of 2000 -- when I think in reality it was 1999, but let's say from 2000, the Kosovo television was a well-fledged [as interpreted] television. After the war I was a spokesperson of the Democratic Party and I was the one who made clear to the public every political stand of the KLA. I took part of the party -- correction. I was a member of the transitional council set up by UNMIK where I represented my party and those meetings served as a mini-parliament, Your Honours. They were the first creations of the institutions in Kosovo. They were broadcast life or in the evening as special features for the citizens of Kosovo, that is, the debates in the transitional council. It was the only council where the main political subjects participated and debated with the representatives of the international community regarding crucial issues in Kosova and other problems.
