There was an administrative counsel as well beside that, which was formed of four political groups, three Albanians and one Serb. And the UNMIK representative. So that was as -- served as a mini-parliament of the transitional council for the citizens of Kosova to follow. That was the first time for them to -- to see what was going on in their television. Things which they hadn't been able to see in Albanian since 1999. And there was several dailies, daily newspapers which appeared, four or five, at that time. I was, in short, of the party spokesperson. Our party was one of the most important parties and I was the one to make public its stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Could I just ask whether -- you did say"things that they hadn't been able to see in Albanian since 1999." Did you mean 1999 or did you mean --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No I meant 1999 -- 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: 1990, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I was wrong. It was--

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It was the interpreter's mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: You mentioned there obviously television and it's newspapers. Did the same apply to radio channels as well in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Sometimes I have participated in some local radio programmes, in addition to the main radio station. I have visited every city who has invited me to unfurl my views, our position. Sometimes I appeared on local television stations. It was after the war. We wanted to speak about our experience. It was in a way a kind of documentary. People were interested in knowing who participated in the war, in knowing the various commanders so I have participated in such programmes. I have had interlocutors and I have talked with viewers about war developments. People wished to know people who participated in the war and to hear from them what they had been through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And of lesser importance but again relevant: Did your photograph appear on posters in Pristina and elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are well versed in democratic experience here. You know very well what an election campaign involves in every country that holds such elections. In our case, in all of the cities of Pristina, all over the town, even outside the town, wherever I participated, I attended various electoral rallies speaking on behalf of my party and I could see the posters all over the place. Like the one I showed, the small one. There is a big poster. Posters like that were placed all over Pristina, I think, with B 1 or B 2 format.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, before we come to the very last situation which was your arrest in 2003, therefore I want to deal just in general terms your thoughts between the end of the war and your arrest about the final status in relation to Kosovo, and your hopes and objectives politically for Kosovo at that time.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our objectives clear, at least mine -- my objectives. They were in conformity with the country's developments in conformity with the developments or even the stand for others. For me Kosovo was in a transitional stage. We needed to build the institutions and want the international community to help us because we started from the scratch. The international institutions came, representatives came to a country tree which lacked everything. We had to begun, as I said, from scratch, from a classical occupation. We had entered a new democratic system which was unknown to us. In the 1990s, Kosovo didn't have the opportunity to develop in a democratic way like the other countries were. So from a classical occupation which lasted for ten years, with all its problems, now we had to pass on to an unknown democratic process for which people were not prepared to take into their hands the leadership of the institutions. And to make this institutions function properly we need the presence of the international community to prepare the Kosovars to be able to take into their hands the leadership of their institutions and to go to the final stages, that of the independence of Kosovo. So my stand was, my orientation, my goal was to go in the direction of establishment of rule of law, democratic state, with strong powerful democratic institutions; to establish a rule of law, create a safe environment and to have the state of the rule of law function properly for to us be prepare the for the final stages in this case, the independence of Kosova. That was our main objective, main objective of my political activity at that time, in close cooperation always with the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And within that what was your attitude towards ethnic minorities within Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My political stance was known. Now I was a person who had made my views publicly known as well as those of my party. Our position towards minority was clear. I have always stated during election campaigns and in rallies we have an example. We have the example of Milosevic, I have always said. If we want to have the same fate as Milosevic, who a dictatorship state, then we know better than anyone what such a state means when you deprive people of their rights when you suppress, use violence against them. So for us we don't need any better example of not doing what we should not do. The other alternative is the one that is presented to us by the international community. We are still a long way from civilised Europe and world and therefore we should undertake the steps to build a free and society where every citizen of Kosova should feel equal and free. This is an objective we have for the future. This is not easy for us because the war had left its imprint. A large number of Serbs had left Kosova with the withdrawal of the forces. Some of them had been involved in the use of violence. So after the entry of the KFOR and the return of 700,000 Albanians who returned to Kosova in a month, refugees from all over, or from places -- or different places they returned finding that their parents, their children had died. Among them there were people who were keen on revenge because they blamed the Serbs for everything that had happened to them. So in this situation, having 700.000 people return in a month to a country which lacked -- practically lacked institutions, which had an institutional vacuum because Serbia pulled out with all of its institutions. So all those who return in this case, those who came in its place, that is the KLA and the UNMIK, they came to a place where they were not prepared to take the lead of the situation. So this vacuum, that chaos that prevailed unfortunately brought about -- produced a lot of pain. There are Serbs but there are also Albanians who were killed during that time who were displaced because of the grave situation after the war. We wanted to heal these consequences. We wanted to convince the Serbs that we are not going to do the same things that the others did, but there was profound distrust. Those human relations we used to have before the war were disrupted. So these needed time to heal. We started negotiations with the Serbs. I think we did good work. I have constant contacts with their representatives in the institutions we had in the provisional council, in parliament, and I think they knew very well what my objectives were. For your information, I think that Serbia had lost even it's moral right in Kosova after what we had done to them. With a fleeing of a million people from Kosova, I think Serbia had no moral right to have any say in Kosova. So we were trying to make it clear to our Serb colleagues to work together, to build Kosova, to have our rights, each of us, but without the influence of that of Belgrade. Even now, even today, I think the Serbs have been under -- they thought that everything had to be done through Belgrade, and I think that they still abide by the same position, despite some positive changes made recently. This is how political developments went, even though we had made clear our objectives, they had their reasons to be -- to feel hesitant because their life was still difficult, most of the Albanians wanted to help them. But the situation of security was, and still is, fluid, just to a large extent. It was difficult for us to build the security institutions. However, I really must believe that if we don't take the initiative of creating, building, trust among us, nothing will succeed, no matter what UNMIK does. I regret it to say, but in this case, in Kosova, we should have Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. brave people, people who are willing to assume responsibilities upon their own shoulders and not to do things only for the sake of the international community, as the case is today in Kosova. With -- we should do things because this is the interest -- for the benefit of the people, not because international community wants us to do that. Standards are for the people, for the citizens; they are the ones who build life. In a word, these were some of the objectives or my orientation. I think that brave politicians, courageous politicians, are still missing in Kosova, politicians who should assume responsibility for the good of the people. But unfortunately, the ones who have -- think only of their own interests, and this has created tension in my country. This is my personal view. I don't want to delve deeper into politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I just want to ask you one more thing on this, and that is really for a personal example of your attitude towards, in this case, a Serb who lived in a flat on the floor above you in Pristina. Is this something that you're able to illustrate in relation to these views that you have expressed?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have stated this in 1999, in 2000 for Free Europe or BBC, where I was interviewed. And I have stated this: That I wished I was not a citizen of Kosova in 1999 because I was ashamed of the developments at that time, because that was not the ideal or the objective of those who fell in the war for the freedom of Kosova. Yesterday I told you that the apartment block where I lived had both Albanians and Serbs as residents. When I returned to Pristina in 1999, I went to my apartment. I visited my father. And having seen the developments, the euphoria, people who had left and coming back and all this, I went to my apartment and I went to the apartment of the Serb living below me. I told him not to leave. I told him that we do not have the means to defend all those who are in Kosova, but I can do this much to defend you who are here, near me. I asked him to stay with us, and I told him that anything that befalls on my family will befall on him, that he would be protected. But he said to me that in those circumstances there was no perspective for him, that he could not stay locked in the apartment. And it was true because I could not guarantee what would happen to him if he walks outside his apartment. Those were the circumstances at that time. His apartment was not touched. I don't know what happened, whether he sold it or whether he rented it himself, but this is just an illustration. At that time, this was the only thing you could do. You couldn't do much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I want to move, finally, therefore, to February, 2003. Again there is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Is Your Honour intending to rise at quarter to 6.00? I was anticipating that might be the break. I can do this subject in that time, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: The -- I think there's no issue that you were on holiday. I want to just ask you about this. Did you go on a short break in February 2003?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a very difficult week in the parliament, at that time I was a member of parliament. We decided together with the president of the party to have a short rest in Slovenia. I went to a skiing centre in Kranjska Gora in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Do you remember the day on which you went, the date -- the date and the day?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be 15th of February. It was Saturday when I left Pristina. Yes, it must be 15th of February. It was Saturday when we left Pristina airport in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Did your family and the authorities know you were leaving?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course that my family knew. I even know that on Friday evening, when we discussed the trip to Slovene, we also spoke with the prime minister at that time, Mr. Bajram Rexhepi, and invited him to join us for the holiday. So the family knew, the entire staff of the democrat party knew. They all knew that they were going to Slovenia. And after all, they knew that we were the leadership of the party and I was in the company of the president of the party. And they all knew that this was not a secret trip. They knew that we were going on a holiday. In short, this was something normal, something that they were aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether you can answer the next question, but did -- are you aware or not as to whether the general in charge of KFOR, General Fabio Mini, also knew that you were going?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't speculate, but if the general was acquainted about the investigations and about the indictment, he surely was aware of my whereabouts. When I left, everything was done in regular basis, officially. The passports were checked in a regular way, as the VIP passports are checked, but I suppose that if the general had the information, he of course knew about our whereabouts. But personally I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: All right. So you leave on Saturday, the 15th. When is it that you first get some wind or knowledge of the fact that people are being arrested or wanted at The Hague? When do you first get some hint of that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arrests were very common in Kosova at that time, for different reasons. If someone is arrested as a result of an indictment issued by The Hague -- I heard about this on Monday while I was on holiday - if I'm not wrong, it was Monday evening - and I heard it from journalists who actually called me to take a statement regarding the new developments in the country. They told me that two or three persons were arrested, and he asked me about the party's opinion on this. So this was it. Then later I heard from friends. I called some friends from the party, and this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now -- first, there are a couple of questions arising out of that First of all, how did the journalists contact you?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The political spokesperson is the one who establishes contacts with the journalists, in order to make the stance of his party known to the public. So the spokesperson lives on the journalist and the journalist lives on the spokesperson. So in order to -- for this to function, you have to have a good relationship with the journalists. All of the journalists in Kosova and journalists from other agencies as well had my phone number. Even the agencies of Serbia, televisions and media, they had business card. My phone number was a public knowledge to all those who had in their hands my business card.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, the other matter is: Were there the names of the two or three persons arrested given to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In Kosova, usually activities are not that transparent. Maybe this was a nature as far as The Hague activity was concerned, but even in Kosova you cannot find out the names of the arrested persons immediately. The journalists, as they always say, according to anonymous sources in UNMIK, they said that these arrested were ordered by the Prosecution in The Hague, and they wanted a statement regarding these developments. I didn't know who the arrested persons were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: When did you --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it out when the names were made public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. When did you discover that in fact you were wanted by the authorities?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want me to describe the entire event, I will tell you that when I heard that my name was mentioned in the indictment and that I was wanted by the Tribunal, I was in a ski-lift. It was around 2.30 or 3.00. A journalist called me, a journalist from Reuters called Shaban Buza. And he said to me, Have you heard what had happened? I said, No. He tried not to touch upon this directly, but when he saw that I had no idea of what he was saying, he then asked me directly. He said that -- so he informed me, not asked me, that Madam del Ponte had given a statement in Podgorica at a press conversation half an hour ago, and she had mentioned your name as one of the accused. Then I said to him, Let me get down first and call me back later in order to read to me the entire statement given by Madam del Ponte. So I got off the ski-lift. He read the entire statement, the press conference statement, and I went to the hotel. I think he was the first journalist who received this information, because he was a journalist of Reuters, and he was the first one to receive the information before the local media received it. And then all journalists began to call me as soon as the news spread in Kosova. Family members called me, friends called me. I couldn't respond to all their calls; it was impossible. I just informed them -- I informed the president of the party, Mr. Thaqi, about the information that we received. We went to the hotel. We contacted the councillor to the prime minister, Mr. Ramadan Ardin, because the prime minister was not available at the time. He must have been on a meeting somewhere. And I said to Ramadan -- I told him to inform the prime minister about this and to -- for the prime minister to consult Mr. Steiner what to do. I wanted personally to return to Kosova and to travel from Kosova to The Hague. However, this was to be arranged by Mr. Steiner, if he was in a position to arrange such a thing. So Ramadan told me that he was going to discuss this with the prime minister, and the prime minister, together with Mr. Krasniqi, a delegation, a small delegation of the party went to meet Mr. Steiner. I don't know when this meeting was held exactly. I was waiting for their response. And while I was waiting, journalists from different media began to call me on the phone. And as it is always with journalists, first thing they want to know is where you are, so that they would be able to contact me directly. My response to them was that I was outside Kosovo. To some I said I was in Austria. To some I didn't tell them at all where I was, and the reason was simple because I had experience with journalists. And I know that in discussions with journalists I could harm myself in respect to what the result of the meeting with Mr. Steiner was going to be. I was sure that if I told them the location where I was, the hotel would be filled up with journalists in five minutes. Therefore, in order to give space to the meeting in Pristina, I didn't tell the journalists the exact location. To some I said that I was at home, busy with a family; to some, I said that I was in Austria, in Italy. I don't know even know myself what I told them exactly, but I know that I didn't tell them the exact place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: You mentioned there Mr. Steiner. Could you indicate who he was?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Steiner at that time was the head of UNMIK at that time. The UN mission to Kosova. He was number one for Kosova at that time. He was president of Kosova. You can call him whatever you like. He was number one and had the authority in Kosova at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And was it made known to him exactly where you were?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no reason for not making it known to him because the prime minister of Kosova with a delegation had gone to him to inform him. I wasn't worried what was going to happen, whether I was going back to Kosova or not. I was worried that what might happen -- I didn't want Mr. Steiner or the delegation to worry about any reaction by the population. If justice called me, I was ready to respond to that justice. So this was my concern, and I wanted to be given the opportunity to address the citizens, that this was something that was made public by the Prosecution; and whether they were right or wrong, this was something to be proved. I didn't want them to dramatise the situation. They were not in a very suitable situation. They didn't know the reaction of my sympathisers. And that's why I wanted the prime minister to go with a clear idea to Mr. Steiner, that -- to tell him that Mr. Limaj is aware of the indictment against him, he is in Slovenia now, today, and he asks you if you can to arrange his return to Kosova without any interruption by the Serbian -- correction, Slovenian authorities. I forgot to tell you, after I heard about the indictment, I asked from an Albanian in Slovenia who was with me, I asked her to ask if there was a plane flying to Pristina on the same night, but there wasn't any flight for Pristina because there are only flights two or three times a week between Pristina and Ljubljana.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So Mr. Steiner, of course he knew I was in Slovenia because what was discussed was whether he was in position to find a charter flight from Ljubljana to Pristina, and then from me to go from Pristina to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield, our tapes are about to run out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. I have only one question, but I can save it. It was: Did you remain where you were and were you arrested in the hotel. That was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You've asked it; he can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I think the answer is yes; it's one of the few leading questions I think -- the only -- well, not the only. Your Honour, I'm sorry we have overrun a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is your answer question, Mr. Limaj, to those questions, you were detained where you were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues ...]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] In a hotel, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn and resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it your examination has concluded, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, it has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, we have some of your questions for you. We have noticed that some of your answers have been long ones. I hope that the few short questions that I have for you will be able to generate short answers and I hope very much that what I have for you will be finished before we rise for this evening. I'm going to take matters in chronological order. Your first meeting with Isak Musliu took place in Likovc, did it not, sometime in April of 1998?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You had never met him before that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. Even that day, on the trip from Likovc, I remember he was silent, unlike Luan who likes to talk like me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Touche. Can I move from April into May, please, Mr. Limaj. The 9th of May in particular saw the moment you described to us when Lapusnik came under attack; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I want to be clear about it, because you described four friends going to the Berisa mountains to secure a better view of what was going on. Do you remember putting it that way when you were answering Mr. Mansfield's questions yesterday?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: One of those friends was Isak Musliu, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Can you help us with the names of the other people who made up that small group?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. In addition to Isak, there was my nephew, Sadik Shala who was a martyr to the nation. There was the cousin to Sadik, his uncle's son, Nexhmaj Shala [phoen], Isak, and someone by the name of Bart [phoen]. I don't remember his last name. He is from Drenoc village. There was a Sadik Shala, my other nephew. We were altogether six people. Sadik was stopped at Berisa with his radio. The five of us continued on the trip to Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Again I want to be absolutely clear about it, if you can help, please, Mr. Limaj. This was, was it not, a collective decision to go and help the villagers of Lapusnik? You nor anyone else in your small group, I suggest, which included my client, were acting under anyone's orders or directions; you simply decided as a group to go and see what you could do to help. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was precisely as I put it. We went out to see what was happening. When we saw what was occurring we decided to go on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Can I deal before I move into June with one matter, as it were on the way, and that is the choice of nom de guerre, pseudonym. We've had evidence from Prosecution witnesses, and I'd like it from you, if you can help us, who indicate that there was a clear self-protective purpose in using pseudonyms, protecting your own identity and protecting the identity of your families. Is that how you saw the purpose of the pseudonym, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the way I described it, it was because of conspiracy. I think you can find the answer in that. Apart from providing security to ourselves and to our families it was for the purposes of not being known and identified. Of course we served the security of our families and ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I want to move, then, for a moment or two into the month of June of 1998. Yesterday you told us - and the reference in the unrevised transcript line if Mr. Whiting wishes it, is page 47, beginning at line 2 - you told us, Mr. Limaj, if you recall, professional soldiers, or former soldiers, a group of three or five of them who came from abroad and joined the KLA. Do you remember telling Mr. Mansfield about that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You said that they'd come, as it were, via the General Staff and were observing the terrain and, as you put it, in line 8 of that page "every unit." I want to deal, if I may, please, with a visit those gentlemen took to Lapusnik. Mr. Limaj, you may not be able to help us because you simply may not be able to recall, but there was an occasion when those officers, two of them perhaps - maybe three - with you, went to Lapusnik in your company and met Isak Musliu. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said yesterday they came in the course of their trip to visit all the units. Lapusnik was an important point. I should say that it was -- in itself it was a special, symbolic, if I might say so because. Lapusnik was the place where the KLA was concentrated so everything liked to go there and visit the units. Some people might pretend today that they weren't there, they never visited the place. But at that time it was considered a treat to go there, in a way. So they visited the units there, in Lapusnik, on the orders -- on the instructions of General Staff to see how the situation was and precisely where -- in the position where Isak was these two officers passed by. They looked at the position, they saw what kind of armaments the soldiers had. The visited last 15 or 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Well, thank you. I was precisely going to suggest upon my instructions exactly that: a visit of about 15 or 20 minutes. And as far as Isak Musliu is concerns, Mr. Limaj, I may this suggestion to you: There was not any other occasion that he recollects through me when such a visit occurred subsequently. Are you aware of any other occasion when those same military officers visited Lapusnik and met with Musliu?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened at the end of June, what I just said. Byslym Zyropi as an officer that we knew when he came at the end of June, he began to visit all of the points. He passed through dangers, sides to Kajxhin [phoen], Suva Reka, Shale. He didn't go back to that point, and I don't where know the August offensive found him. Agim was killed immediately, after a week in Rahovec so...

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Can I in fact come on to Rahovec, Mr. Limaj, please and we move therefore move chronologically into July.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yesterday at transcript page 69, to be exact, you said: "Rahovec mirrors the way the KLA was organised at that time." Mr. Limaj, may I make an alternative suggestion as to a rephrasing of your evidence: Rahovec mirrors the way the KLA was disorganised at that time. Do you accept that as a proposition?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I would put it differently. Rahovec shows that the KLA was still a long way from being -- from being responsive to the new reality. It had remained still under total confusion, a guerrilla unit. Because to disorganised first you have to be organised, I think. But it was not organised to be disorganised. I don't know if I made myself clear. Maybe I am putting it in the same way you put it to me, but in different words.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, it's for the Chamber to reach those decisions, Mr. Limaj, but I think the flavour of what I'm suggesting to you has come over in your answer. There is one particularly important matter I want to deal with regarding Rahovec, if I may, and that is something that you did not mention yesterday and again I want to see if you agree. That on the 19th of July - I can't put a time on the day, I'm afraid - you met Isak Musliu there, or thereabouts and you were with Byslym Zyropi. Now, you don't mention Musliu yesterday when Mr. Mansfield was asking you about this. I am positively suggesting to that you Musliu was there and you met with him and indeed discussed or he was part of a discussion, regarding the tactical decisions that needed to be made. So let me break that long question up. First of all, do you agree he was there?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth I didn't mention his name because I concentrated on describing the representatives of the General Staff. That's why I have forgotten to mention his name. I wanted to point out the fact that the decision was made by the -- the people who came from the General Staff didn't know that. But it is true that Isak was there. But for me it was not an important thing to mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It was -- he won't mind me mentioning this on his behalf. He was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. not a significant a figure militarily such as others such as Mr. Zyropi and other members of the General Staff. That's a fair description, is it not, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Indeed, he wasn't alone, was he in, as it were, being from a series of volunteers who responded to urgent radio request for assistance to come to Rahovec. Others answered the same call, did they not?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the 18th and 19th there were no units, no soldiers from Drenice, from Dukagjine, from Malisheve, they came. Hundreds of people came to Rahovec to help. There was total confusion so everybody wanted to give a hand. They came from all sides, groups of soldiers. And in that situation you couldn't tell who was coming from where and what was doing and in that situation my nephew got killed, Sadik. He thought that I was injured and he entered on one side and he got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I don't suppose you could assist, Mr. Limaj, can you - you would have had other things on your mind to deal with - as to how long Isak Musliu may have spent in that area in the days following the 19th. Can you assist at all?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th, after I had that -- suffered that shock, and was taken to the hospital, I don't know what happened afterwards. Because the news spread out, Your Honours, to Malisheve that someone was injured and someone was killed and that -- I know that after my stay in hospital for some hours when I regained consciousness, I tried to go home to -- because I knew that the news about my death was -- had reached my family. I wanted them to know that I was still alive. So the news was spread all over Malisheve because they had seen me lying down in the car. And I went to Banje, stayed my family -- then went back to Klecke to rest. But I may tell you that on the 19th and 20th and 21st, Isak was not in Rahovec but between Rahovec and Malisheve. Because at that time the Serbian forces had taken Rahovec and we were thinking what to do to prevent them from enters Malisheve, because they thought that the Serb offensive would continue in the direction of Malisheve. So we wanted to block the way and this is where I saw Isak.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I was going to actually suggest to you that subsequent to the 19th Isak and others position themselves on a small hill near Rahovec and stayed in or about that position for the following four and a half days or so. Now, I don't suppose you can be that precise. But the essence of what I think you just said appears to accept that he was in that area for several days following the 19th. Did you agree?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I said it. After the 19th. Because on the 19th Rahovec was in chaos. In the evening of the 17th, 18th, the Serbian forces had entered. So the soldiers left Rahovec and took positions between Rahovec and Malisheve. On the 22nd, 23rd, all of them stayed along that line thinking that the Serbian troops would continue towards Malisheve. They wanted to protect the hundreds and thousands of civilians behind their back. They wanted to bar the way to the Serbs to continue towards Malisheve. There were many soldiers there. The members of the General Staff, Rexhep Selimi, Hashim Thaqi all of them were there with the soldiers during these days, from the 19th to the 23rd, between Rahovec and Malisheve, to coordinate activities and to prevent the entry of the Serbian troops. Not to suffer a new defeat. Because we were worried about the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I follow. I want to break off the chronology and, as it were, insert something else here for a moment, Mr. Limaj. The nom de guerre, the pseudonym that Isak Musliu had by then was Qerqizi, was it not?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Are you aware of how it was that he was given that name, by, I suggest, Ismet Jashari? Are you aware? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: My suggestion is that he looked like the famous national hero Qerqizi Topulli. Is that right, Mr. Limaj, or is it some other reason?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Qerqizi Topulli was famous for many things, including his beard, Mr. Limaj. He was a bearded figure in history, wasn't he? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. That was his particularity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Isak Musliu, Mr. Limaj, in the time we have just been dealing with was the wearer of a significant beard, wasn't he? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Can we move on from Rahovec back to Lapusnik, because you have told Their Honours that you were hurt, injured, ill. I think you have used those words. I want to ask you to just turn to your left to look - and I'm grateful, for the usher has pinned DM3 to the wall. I hope it might be a convenient way of doing it. Mr. Limaj, on the evening of the 25th of July you were, I suggest, in the Sopi neighbourhood of the village of Lapusnik receiving medical treatment and in particular, I suggest, you were lying down with an IV drip in your arm, an intravenous drip. Now again, I will break it up. First of all, do you accept that on the 25th of July you were back in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You may not know the district or the village that you were in. I'm going to ask -- see if we can identify it in a minute. Do you know the district, name of the village or the district that you were in or not?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know. Because I had lost consciousness. I didn't know exactly to which house they took me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: An IV drip suggests that there may have been some medical intervention at the time. Were you being treated by a doctor or a nurse or what?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me it was quite a haze. I thought that Dr. Zeqaj [phoen] was the one, but Ferat Sopi was serving too as an assistant or nurse, as well as two other nurses. I thought that Zeqaj was a doctor. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Now would you mind looking to your left you will see a number --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Perhaps it could be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, it would be easier because Mr. Whiting can't see it from there. Yes, forgive me. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, you will he recollect that during the Prosecution case a Prosecution witness provided us with this piece of material. Could I draw your attention to first of all the five positions of the Celiku 3 unit that Mr. Mansfield was talking to you about yesterday, I think. And then when you come down to position number 4, if you just move, as it were, towards the centre of the photograph. You will see a label that has a Q against it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I don't how distinct it is on Your Honours' screens. It is incredibly indistinct on mine. Your Honours, against the fourth label down --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, in fact what we can do, Mr. Limaj, is I can locate the grid. Can you see what I am talking about? Can you identify the grid, please. You'll see grid numbers at the top or letters at the top and numbers down the side.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues...] is it in?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: C4. I'm grateful. Now, I know it's difficult from aerial photographs, and I'm sure everyone understands the difficulty. What I've put to a previous witness was that was one of the bases, houses, in that area there where Musliu was based for a while. Mr. Limaj, what I'm going to suggest to you is: That that is the area of the village where you may well have been and the town - and I put it deliberately carefully like that - on the night of the 25th because I'm going to suggest to you that Isak Musliu saw you with the IV drip in your arm, and I'll put it compendiumly [sic] and then you deal with it in bits. You told us yesterday, transcript page 62, that 8.00 in the evening of the 25th [sic] you were told of the death of Ymer Alushani or thereabouts. Now, I'll break it up. First of all, that area of the village, could that be where you were or can't you help us?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to say that we were intent on going to the front line, but because of the insistent shelling by the Serbs it was very difficult indeed to penetrate into the military positions. In a meadow somewhere here, I had that loss of consciousness that I mentioned, and two or three soldiers of course took me to a nearby home. And those soldiers know better than me when I stayed. It was -- fighting was going on; there was an offensive. In the evening when it became dark they took me away from that place. It is possible. But for me, as I said, it's all a haze.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me. I think counsel may have misspoken. I think that the evidence, as I read it from page 62, is that it's 8.00 in the evening on the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. Oh, is it? Yes, I see what Mr. Whiting says. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: 26th, Mr. Limaj, 8.00 you told us yesterday Isak came round. Is it your recollection that Isak Musliu was the one who told you that Ymer Alushani had been killed?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard some voices. Nobody knew what was going on. Some soldiers were speaking, but I heard from him what had happened because he had seen with his own eyes what had happened and he was describing the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: We don't need the ELMO any more. Thank you. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I can move on, Mr. Limaj, in the 15 minutes or so that's left. I'm confident --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry to rise again. I'm sorry. Is -- was that an exhibit that was shown to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: DM3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: DM3. Okay. I wasn't sure that was clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: DM03, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Can I move on, please, into August. Again today you described in some detail the formation of the 121st Brigade, and you put it, if I'm accurately noting what you said, on or about the 6th of August that there was a meeting of a number of commanders at which you said, and I accept, Isak Musliu was present. Now do you remember those answers to Mr. Mansfield a little earlier on today, in fact, the very beginning of today?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Can I just put a little flesh on that bone, please, Mr. Limaj, and ask you this: Do you accept that this meeting took place in a house in Klecka?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And I can be quite detailed about this. It began at approximately 10.00 in the evening; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, at my base in Klecka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: We've seen a video footage of that base today?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And on the agenda, not surprisingly, I suggest, given the circumstances, was the position of the civilian population; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And the meeting quickly turned, did it not, to discussions regarding the next steps, as it were, which led quickly to discussions regarding the formation of brigades. Do you agree with that as a description of how the meeting went?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The meeting broke up some hours later with quite a finale, I suggest, Mr. Limaj - I put this to someone else who couldn't quite remember, so let's see if you can. Three mortar rounds landed near the house towards the end of the meeting. Do you remember that? You smile. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I forgot to mention many things here, but of course I remember that we had to stop this meeting because of the shelling. As I said earlier, there was uninterrupted shelling of Klecka, but this one was very near the base and we were forced to stop the meeting and leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, may I just add a little detail to the battalion formation because it's right, isn't it, as you told us this afternoon that Isak Musliu, as it were, found himself promoted that night from whatever he was as that night to -- subsequently to become a deputy brigade commander. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And your other deputy because Ismet Jashari; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ismet Jashari, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Then for completeness's sake, Mr. Limaj, there were four battalions, were there not, formed to be part of the 121st Brigade, and I'm going to name them in a moment. But, first of all, do you agree with the figure, four?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of battalions was a process. It wasn't decided on this point because the units had to be integrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. You're quite right, forgive me. I didn't want to suggest that these battalions were formed that night. But in due course, what we saw developing in this post-first-week-of-August period, between now, I suggest, and the autumn of 1998 were the Ymer Alushani Battalion based on the Berisa Mountainside; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you want me, I can even tell you what the boundary was that we agreed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: If Mr. Whiting wants to ask you about that, he can; I don't, Mr. Limaj, but thank you for the offer. The Ruzhdi Salihu Battalion on the Kroimire side led by Ramiz Qeriqi, a witness from whom we've heard in this case. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ramiz Qeriqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The Sadik Shala Battalion under the command of Ismet Jashari?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And finally the Ymer Kastrati Battalion led by Skender Hoti. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not Ymer Kastrati; it's Afrim Krasniqi, the battalion which was led by Skender Hoti.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I move on then finally, Mr. Limaj, to deal with the last aspect I want to deal with and that is the military police. You tell Mr. Mansfield and us earlier that in 1999 when you had become a member of the General Staff, you were appointed chief of the military police prior to, as I understand your evidence, your appointment as Deputy Minister of Defence. Have I understood your evidence correctly?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need to explain myself here. In a way, no, because, Your Honours, at that time we had received the organisational chart by NATO. One of these departments was the military police. I was appointed by the General Staff general chief of the military police in December of 1998, at the beginning of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Isak Musliu became an important figure in the military police himself, did he not, in 1999?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, every zone later on became to be built-up. We began to unify the way the zones were structured, as it was foreseen with the organisational chart. So the zone had its commander and the commander of the military police, who was under the orders of the commander of the operational zone. So with the proposal of the commander of the Nerodime Operational Zone, Mr. Shukri Buja, he was then appointed commander of the military police for the Nerodime Operational Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Thank you very much. I showed a number of witnesses during the course of the trial, Mr. Limaj, I'm sure you recollect, a photograph of a number of people wearing black uniforms with the PU insignia. Do you remember the photograph? I can show you again, but I don't think we need to see it. You recall? The suggestion I make, Mr. Limaj, is this, and I ask you it in your given capacity as chief of the military police at the time -- the suggestion I make is this: Did those uniforms, those black uniforms with those insignia, did not emerge to be seen by the public, as it were, in Kosova until the back end of 1998 at the earliest. Now do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the pictures you have shown, it's different, but I can explain how it looked, the military police, because I was directly involved. It was a task of the directorate. Your Honours, after August the military police had started to operate and had started to be different from zone to zone. They were made different by their uniforms, by the insignia, even by the tasks that they exercised in their respective zones. So as chief of military police, I asked as an immediate, urgent, issue to be treated before the General Staff to establish a unified uniform for the military police so that all the military police units in every zone had the same uniform, a unified insignia, and to have ID cards. These were the three proposals that I made, and these proposals were to be carried out by the directorate, because that was the duty of the directorate, to contact the commanders of the zones, because every zone had organised themselves in their own way and to their own means. The first thing that we did -- on the market you could find leather jackets from Turkey that were brought there by tradesmen. They were short jackets, and jeans, black jeans, which were produced in Kosova, tailored by Kosovar tailors. So we combined them and formed this uniform. And every military police was obliged to wear this leather jacket and these black jeans. And we took the sign for the military police according to the sign that the NATO military police was using, the same design.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Two things very quickly, Mr. Limaj, if you wouldn't mind. First of all, in what month of the year of 1998, if I have the right year, would one have first seen these uniforms that you just described on the streets, as it were? What month?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could have happened, first of all, for the soldiers in Pastrik Operational Zone sometime in the second half of December of 1998, and then it continued with other zones in January and after January.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I can't remember the witness's name now for the life of me, but we have seen a photograph of a Prosecution witness with a gun in his hand and a bandolero across his chest, wearing -- not an entirely black, but a partly black uniform -- it may be Mr. Karpuzi, I'm not sure -- yes, Mr. Karpuzi, that's right. Did people wear black uniforms, partially black or wholly black in the earlier parts of 1998, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean soldiers, this happened mostly after the 29th of May, when Malisheve was a free territory, and in lack of uniforms people wanted to get themselves singled out to be known as being members of the KLA. And in order to be distinct from citizens, they designed clothes that resembled uniforms. The easiest way to do this was to buy a shirt and pair of trousers because you could not wear white shirts and trousers, that was not practical; that's why they bought dark-coloured, black-coloured shirts and trousers. You could find soldiers dressed in this way in all the area, those who didn't have actual uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you for your help and your patience, Mr. Limaj. That's all I ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Topolski, and that seems a convenient time. We will -- as counsel will be aware, tomorrow is a day when we are unable to sit because of a need to do technical maintenance in the courtroom, so we will resume on Monday at 2.15 and we must therefore adjourn now until Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 23rd of May, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.58 p.m.,
